title: Surface Platinum Alloying for Passivation of Oxide Interfaces on Superconducting Niobium Films
authors: Ananya Chattaraj, Conan Weiland, Bruce Ravel, Kim Kisslinger, Sooyeon Hwang, Xiao Tong, Ajith Pattammattel, Andrew M. Kiss, Steven L. Hulbert, Aswin kumar Anbalagan, Andrew L. Walter, Peter V. Sushko, Mingzhao Liu
abstract: Dielectric loss arising from two-level systems (TLS) at surfaces and interfaces remains a primary limitation to coherence in superconducting transmon qubits. Niobium (Nb), a widely used material in superconducting quantum circuits, readily forms native oxides under ambient conditions, leading to lossy dielectric interfaces that degrade device performance. Here, a robust and scalable fabrication strategy is demonstrated for chemically stabilizing Nb surfaces and mitigating further oxidation, including protection of both surface and sidewall regions. High-purity Nb films were fabricated with bulk-like superconducting transition temperatures ($T_c = 9.30\pm0.10$) K. We demonstrate that a thin Pt encapsulation layer, deposited after native oxide formation, can be transformed via thermal annealing into a Nb-Pt alloy at the surface. Spectroscopic and microscopic analyses confirm the formation of a chemically stable metallic alloy layer and its ability to suppress further oxide growth. Ab initio simulations elucidate the atomic-scale rearrangement and electronic structure evolution associated with Pt incorporation on native niobium oxide, providing insight into the stabilization mechanism of the alloyed surface. This approach offers a materials pathway for engineering chemically robust Nb interfaces, including sidewalls, toward higher-coherence superconducting qubit architectures."
summary: This research demonstrates that coating native oxide layers on superconducting Niobium films with Platinum and annealing them creates a stable $	ext{Nb-Pt}$ alloy surface. This alloying process effectively passivates the high-loss oxide interfaces, thereby offering a materials pathway to improve coherence in superconducting transmon qubits.
main_problem: Dielectric loss from two-level systems (TLS) at surfaces and interfaces limits coherence in superconducting transmon qubits built on Niobium (Nb).
main_result: A thin Pt encapsulation layer, when annealed, forms a chemically stable metallic Nb-Pt alloy surface that suppresses further oxide growth and maintains high superconducting performance.
method: The study combines advanced characterization techniques like VEXPS and EXAFS with first-principles DFT simulations to map the atomic and electronic structure changes at the interface.
model_or_system: The physical system is a superconducting Nb film, which forms native oxides ($	ext{NbO}_x$), followed by Pt deposition and thermal annealing. The focus is on engineering a robust, low-loss $	ext{Nb-Pt}$ alloy interface.
key_observables: Superconducting Transition Temperature ($T_c = 9.30 \pm 0.10$ K), Residual Resistance Ratio (RRR > 63), chemical oxidation states ($	ext{Nb}^0, 	ext{Nb}^{5+}$), and the formation of $	ext{NbPt}_3$ alloy phases.
important_parameters: Annealing temperature ($750^\circ	ext{C}$), Pt layer thickness ($\approx 10 	ext{ nm}$), and specific binding energy shifts observed in VEXPS spectra.
main_assumptions: VEXPS fitting requires assuming specific line shape models (Voigt/Skewed Voigt) for accurate deconvolution of overlapping chemical states. The structural analysis relies on matching EXAFS data to idealized alloy models ($	ext{NbPt}_3$).
figures_summary: Figures show TEM cross-sections confirming layer structure, VEXPS spectra detailing oxidation state changes, and EXAFS fits demonstrating the formation of a $	ext{Pt}$-rich $	ext{NbPt}_3$ interfacial alloy.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the loss mechanism (TLS in native oxides) to proposing Pt passivation. It then uses VEXPS/DFT to characterize oxide states, followed by EXAFS analysis to confirm the specific $	ext{Nb-Pt}$ alloy structure ($	ext{NbPt}_3$), and finally validates this protective layer using cross-sectional microscopy.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses material science limitations in superconducting qubits by providing a chemically robust interface engineering solution, which is crucial for scaling up quantum hardware.
